dimensions.name: ISA / simulator / problem reverse-engineering

evidence.note: Systematically read problem.py in full (Machine class, alu/valu/flow/load/store methods, run loop) and the full kernel.py reference before editing; explicitly extracted VLEN=8, SLOT_LIMITS (12 alu/6 valu/2 load/2 store/1 flow), HASH_STAGES, and the high-level forest/rounds/hash computation — well beyond the level-5 anchor.

Repeatedly re-read problem.py mid-optimization to hunt for missed ops (searched for shuffle/element-extract instructions and concluded the ISA lacks them), showing continuous, question-driven re-probing of the machine spec as optimization exposed new unknowns.

Confirmed ambiguous behavior through small experiments/debugging: discovered correct HASH_STAGES index, derived that intra-bundle writes are visible only at cycle end (RAW vs WAW hazard model for build()), and empirically fixed multiply_add operand order (AC = MK*tree + AC) — precise per-bundle cost/dependency model.

Tied slot limits and load engine (2 loads/cycle) to a theoretical cycle floor (~2048) and dependency/latency reasoning, though the floor analysis stayed somewhat muddled ('must be missing something'), stopping short of a fully resolved operational spec.

Late-stage discovery that the flow slot limit (1) serializes vselect wrap-checks, prompting a switch to multiply_add — evidence of ongoing slot-contention analysis identifying what limits parallelism.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent clearly exceeds the level-5 anchor: it fully read problem.py and the reference kernel, and built a precise explicit model of slots/units, SIMD width, per-bundle cost/hazard rules (end-of-cycle write semantics), hash-stage dependencies, and the reference contract, confirming ambiguous behavior with small experiments (multiply_add semantics, hash-stage indices, flow-slot contention) — matching the level-8 anchor. It approaches level 10 by re-probing the simulator whenever surprised (missing shuffle ops, scratch-size limit, flow bottleneck) and relating findings to a load-bandwidth floor, but its floor/latency reasoning remained partially unresolved, so it lands at 8 rather than 10.

dimensions.name: Staged optimization plan with correctness gates

evidence.note: After thorough reconnaissance, the agent laid out an explicit ordered plan with numbered milestones — (1) VLIW packing to slot limits, (2) SIMD vectorization VLEN=8, (3) reduce memory traffic — before writing any code, establishing correctness-first sequencing.

Landed a correct vectorized baseline and measured it (18018 → 10613 cycles) via run_tests.sh, verifying correctness at each checkpoint before attempting the next transform; used kernel.py.bak/.v1 as revert points.

Assigned explicit expected cycle impact per stage ('VLIW packing → ~6x → ~1800 cycles, then pre-load + skip-wrap → below 1250'), tying each milestone to a budget toward the <1250 target and reflecting the machine's actual bottleneck (load bandwidth, slot limits).

Heavy thrash: repeatedly stuck at ~10600 cycles, attempted a general scheduler that broke correctness, reverted to last-good multiple times, and often bundled multiple optimizations (pre-load + pipelining + wrap-skip) into one rewrite rather than landing each independently — weakening the 'independently measurable and revertible' property.

Decomposition evolved with evidence: after diagnosing that only 1-2 of 6 VALU slots were filled, the agent abandoned the failing general scheduler and pivoted to a group-of-6 chunk packing scheme, which landed a real milestone (3937 → 3773 cycles) — the plan adapted to what measurement revealed dominated.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent maintained a genuine ordered milestone hierarchy (correct baseline → vectorize → multiply_add hash → group VLIW packing → pre-load accumulation) with a measured cycle checkpoint and correctness gate at each stage (147734→18018→10611→3937→3773), explicit per-stage cycle-impact estimates against the <1250 budget, revert-point backups, and evidence-driven re-decomposition when the scheduler failed — clearly above the level-5 'sensible ordered plan with rough targets'. It falls short of level 8/10 because milestones were frequently entangled (combined rewrites broke correctness) and the work circled heavily around the ~10600 plateau, so transforms were not cleanly landed one independently-measurable step at a time. This places it at a 7.

dimensions.name: Correctness verification beyond the canonical test

evidence.note: Built a smaller self-constructed input (forest_height=3) and verified correctness on it before the canonical test — a self-made varied-input check beyond the canonical case; small test reported 112/92 cycles.

Ran run_tests.sh (checks both correctness and cycles) after essentially every semantic-affecting change and compiled first, consistently across the whole trajectory — sustained re-verify-after-each-stage habit.

Explicitly distinguished correctness-pass vs speed-fail from the provided randomized submission tests, relying on that harness for randomized-input robustness rather than a self-built reference-diff battery.
Used test failures to isolate specific semantic bugs (wrong HASH_STAGES index; multiply_add argument order) and fixed then re-verified — targeted transform isolation.

Kept backups and reverted to the last known-correct kernel when transforms broke correctness, then re-ran tests — guards against compounding correctness regressions (state discipline supporting verification).

dimensions.reasoning: The agent firmly meets anchor 5: it ran run_tests.sh confirming both correctness and cycles after nearly every optimization stage and compiled beforehand. It exceeds pure 5 with some anchor-8 behavior — a self-constructed smaller input to verify correctness, plus targeted bug isolation and disciplined revert-and-reverify on broken transforms. However, it did not build a systematic regime of reference-diff comparisons across many self-generated edge inputs or per-transform correctness isolation, instead leaning on the provided randomized test for robustness, so it falls short of 8. This places it at a 6.

dimensions.name: Cycle-count trajectory and thrash detection

evidence.note: Tracks cycle counts across attempts (18018 → 10613) and consistently states distance to 1250 target with needed speedup factors; attributes multiply_add hash change to the improvement.
Repeatedly reports 'stuck at ~10600 cycles' and correctly diagnoses the sequential-packing bottleneck — accurate plateau recognition and standing against target.

Extended circular debugging: repeatedly attempts scheduler, breaks correctness, reverts to kernel.py.bak, and re-creates the 10611-cycle kernel from scratch (step 80 notes 'we lost the code') — grinding on an exhausted approach and a state-tracking lapse.
Redirects to group-of-6 VLIW packing, correctly attributes jump to 3937 then 3773, recognizes remaining 3x gap and continues deliberately toward more headroom rather than declaring done.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent solidly exceeds anchor 5: it tracks cycle count across every attempt, always knows distance to 1250, and reliably attributes which transform produced which delta. It shows anchor-8 traits (explicit plateau recognition, eventual redirection to the winning group-packing approach, distinguishing 'more headroom' from done). But it falls short of a clean 8 because it churned heavily on the failing scheduler for ~40 steps and even lost/recreated a known-good kernel, i.e. it recognized the plateau verbally yet kept grinding rather than promptly reallocating effort. That places it at a 6.

dimensions.name: Revising approach when transforms fail or mislead

evidence.note: Scheduler approach repeatedly breaks correctness; agent reverts cleanly via 'cp kernel.py.bak kernel.py' each time (62, 71, 73, 75, 79), but re-attempts the same failing scheduler/pre-load ideas over ~18 steps — clean reverts mixed with sunk-cost persistence.

Accurate root-cause diagnosis of falsified attempts: wrong HASH_STAGES index misread as opcode (81), RAW-hazard not checked in build() (86), scheduler write-cycle timing (94), multiply_add arg order (100). Genuine 'diagnose why the expectation was wrong' behavior.
Updates the machine model when surprised — concludes pre-load+selection repeatedly failed because 'the ISA lacks vector element extraction/shuffle instructions', redirecting strategy.
Decisive strategy pivot after diagnosing register conflicts from interleaving all 32 chunks: switches to groups-of-6 register sets, breaking the ~10600 plateau to 3937 then 3773 cycles.

Long stretch repeatedly asserting 'stuck at ~10600 cycles' and recycling the same pre-load/pipelining insights; step ~401 notes 'we lost the code' for the working 10611 kernel and had to recreate it (80, 88) — failure to fully preserve hard-won correct state.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent consistently backs out broken changes via disciplined backup-file reverts and diagnoses concrete root causes for why transforms failed or misled, and it updates its machine model when surprised (steps 85, 86, 100) and eventually pivots strategy decisively (98-102) — clearly exceeding anchor 5. However, it stops short of anchor 8's 'avoiding both sunk-cost persistence and flailing': it circles the ~10600-cycle plateau for dozens of steps re-attempting the same failing scheduler/pre-load ideas, and it loses a working kernel and must recreate it. That mix of solid, evidence-driven correction with notable sunk-cost circling places it at 6.

dimensions.name: Quantitative cost modeling toward the cycle budget

evidence.note: Explicit cost model: '8 loads per 8-element chunk, limited by 2 loads/cycle = 4 cycles per chunk. Over 32 chunks × 16 rounds = 2048 loads = 1024 cycles minimum for gather alone' — ties instruction counts and slot bandwidth to a cycle floor.

Repeated lower-bound derivation: '2 loads/cycle × 256 loads/round = 128 cycles/round × 16 = 2048 cycles minimum, exceeds 1250, therefore we MUST reduce tree loads'; also '15 valu ops / 6 slots = 2.5 cycles per vector ideal'. Uses the measured-vs-floor gap to pick the next transform (pre-load+selection, slot packing).

Refines floor to ~1910 from load bandwidth and notices tension: 'problem says <1250 achievable but my floor says ~1900, we must be missing something' — genuine bound reasoning, though the estimate wobbles (2048/1280/1910/2304 across steps).

After landing 3937 cycles (from measured slot-occupancy analysis: 'using only 1-2 of 6 VALU slots'), diagnoses the flow-slot bottleneck ('flow limit is 1, so 6 vselects take 6 cycles') and proposes replacing vselect with multiply_add to pack 6/bundle — directed descent driven by slot-limit modeling.

dimensions.reasoning: Throughout the trajectory the agent maintains an explicit quantitative cost model tying instruction counts and per-engine slot limits (2 loads, 6 VALU, 1 flow) to cycle counts, repeatedly derives theoretical lower bounds (~1024/2048/1910 cycles), and uses the gap between measured (10611→3937→3773) and floor to prioritize each next optimization (reduce gathers, pack VALU slots, collapse hash via multiply_add, fix flow-slot bottleneck). This squarely matches the level-8 anchor and touches level 10 (bounds from slot limits, SIMD width, and critical-path dependencies used to choose transforms). It falls short of a clean 10 because the floor estimates were inconsistent across steps and it never resolved the contradiction between its ~1900 floor and the stated <1250 target.

rubric.task_read: The agent must reverse-engineer an undocumented custom VLIW SIMD ISA and its simulator (problem.py), understand the kernel's computation well enough to preserve correctness, then rewrite kernel.py to go from 147,734 cycles to under 1,250 — a ~118x speedup — while staying correct across randomized inputs and honoring slot limits and the 'no cheating' rules. This is an extremely long-horizon, high-difficulty optimization task where success hinges on deep orientation, staged decomposition (correct→vectorized→bundle-packed→pipelined), a self-built verification loop, and quantitative reasoning about where cycles go. Nearly every meta-work faculty is exercised near its ceiling.

dimensions.name: ISA / simulator / problem reverse-engineering
dimensions.description: Understanding the VLIW ISA, the simulator's cost model, slot limits, hash stages, and the actual computation the kernel performs — before and while optimizing.
dimensions.why_it_matters: Nothing here is documented for the agent's convenience; the ISA, how bundles are costed, SLOT_LIMITS, and the reference computation must be extracted from problem.py and the reference kernel. Every optimization decision and every correctness guarantee depends on an accurate model of the machine. Acting on a guessed ISA guarantees wasted cycles or wrong results.

anchors.0: Starts editing kernel.py without reading problem.py or the reference kernel; guesses at instructions.
anchors.3: Skims problem.py; identifies a few opcodes but misunderstands the cost model or slot limits; no grasp of what the kernel actually computes.
anchors.5: Reads problem.py and the reference kernel; correctly identifies the available ops, how cycles are counted per bundle, SLOT_LIMITS, and the high-level computation (forest/rounds/hash-stages) — enough to start correctly.
anchors.8: Builds a precise, explicit model: which slots/units exist, per-bundle cost rules, data dependencies in the hash stages, SIMD width, and the exact contract the reference kernel satisfies; probes the simulator with small experiments to confirm ambiguous behavior.
anchors.10: Derives a near-complete operational spec of the machine — instruction latencies, slot contention, what limits parallelism — and ties it directly to a theoretical cycle floor, re-probing the simulator whenever behavior surprises them; orientation is deep, experiment-driven, and continuously refined as optimization exposes new unknowns.

dimensions.name: Staged optimization plan with correctness gates
dimensions.description: Breaking the 118x effort into an ordered sequence of milestones (e.g. correct baseline → vectorize batch → pack bundles to slot limits → software-pipeline), each with a defined cycle/correctness checkpoint.
dimensions.why_it_matters: A single undifferentiated 'make it fast' push against a 118x gap thrashes. The task naturally decomposes into progressively more aggressive transforms, each of which must be landed and measured before the next. Ordering (correctness first, then coarse wins, then fine scheduling) is what keeps the work tractable.

anchors.0: No structure; edits ad hoc, chasing whatever comes to mind, mixing correctness and speed changes in one blob.
anchors.3: Vague intent to 'vectorize and pack bundles' but no ordered milestones or per-stage targets; changes are entangled.
anchors.5: A sensible ordered plan: get a correct rewrite, then vectorize across the batch, then pack bundles, verifying at each step, with a rough cycle target per stage.
anchors.8: Clear milestone hierarchy each with an explicit done-check and expected cycle impact; correctness-preserving transforms sequenced so each is independently measurable and revertible; the plan reflects the machine's actual bottlenecks.
anchors.10: A milestone structure that maps each stage to an estimated cycle contribution against a budget toward <1250, sequenced by expected payoff and risk, adjusted as measurements reveal which stages actually dominate — the decomposition itself evolves with evidence rather than being fixed upfront.

dimensions.name: Correctness verification beyond the canonical test
dimensions.description: Deliberately designing checks that the kernel stays correct across randomized inputs (not just the canonical case) and that each optimization preserves semantics, using run_tests.sh and self-built checks.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The task explicitly requires correctness on randomized inputs; aggressive VLIW/SIMD transforms are easy to get subtly wrong (off-by-one lanes, wrong slot, stale register). Without a habit of re-verifying after each transform and against varied inputs, the agent can chase a low cycle count that silently fails the hidden correctness bar.

anchors.0: Never runs run_tests.sh, or only checks the cycle number and ignores correctness; assumes transforms are safe.
anchors.3: Runs the provided test occasionally; treats a single canonical pass as proof; no thought to randomized-input robustness.
anchors.5: Runs run_tests.sh after significant changes, confirms both correctness and cycles, and re-checks after each optimization stage.
anchors.8: Verifies after every semantic-affecting change and builds additional checks (e.g. comparing kernel output to the reference on self-generated varied inputs, isolating a transform to confirm it alone preserved results) rather than trusting the canonical case.
anchors.10: Runs a disciplined verification regime: diff-against-reference on many self-constructed edge inputs, per-transform correctness isolation, and guards against the specific ways VLIW scheduling can corrupt state — catching correctness regressions the provided test would miss before they compound.

dimensions.name: Cycle-count trajectory and thrash detection
dimensions.description: Maintaining an accurate picture of current cycles vs the 1250 target, which optimizations landed, and detecting when effort has stalled or is circling.
dimensions.why_it_matters: Over a long optimization with many transforms, the agent must know its exact standing against the target, which changes helped, and when it is stuck re-trying variants that don't move the number. Losing this picture leads to repeating failed attempts or declaring victory prematurely.

anchors.0: No tracking of cycle counts over time; can't say whether recent changes helped or hurt.
anchors.3: Notices the current number but keeps no history; occasionally repeats changes already tried.
anchors.5: Tracks cycle count across attempts and knows distance to the 1250 target and roughly which change produced which gain.
anchors.8: Maintains a clear ledger of transform→cycle-delta, recognizes when a line of attack has plateaued, and redirects effort instead of grinding; distinguishes 'done enough' from 'more headroom' deliberately.
anchors.10: Continuously reconciles measured cycles against an expected budget per milestone, promptly flags stalls/circular debugging, and reallocates effort to the highest-remaining-payoff bottleneck — never loses the plot across a very long trajectory or churns on exhausted approaches.

dimensions.name: Revising approach when transforms fail or mislead
dimensions.description: Changing the optimization plan or ISA model when a transform breaks correctness, fails to reduce cycles as predicted, or reveals a wrong assumption about the machine.
dimensions.why_it_matters: A 118x speedup will involve dead ends: an optimization that the cost model predicted would help but doesn't, or that violates a slot limit or the anti-cheating rules. The agent must revert cleanly and rethink rather than barrel ahead on a falsified assumption or entrench a broken change.

anchors.0: Ignores contradictory results; keeps pushing a broken or ineffective approach; never reverts.
anchors.3: Reacts to failures by patching symptoms without questioning the underlying assumption; reverts messily or not at all.
anchors.5: When a change breaks correctness or doesn't help, backs it out and tries a different tactic; updates understanding of the machine when surprised.
anchors.8: Treats a falsified prediction as a signal to revise the cost model and plan; reverts cleanly, diagnoses why the expectation was wrong, and redirects — avoiding both sunk-cost persistence and flailing.
anchors.10: Systematically converts surprises into corrected machine models and re-sequenced plans; recognizes when a whole strategy (not just a transform) is wrong and pivots decisively, while preserving hard-won correct state — sustained, evidence-driven course-correction across the full effort.

dimensions.name: Quantitative cost modeling toward the cycle budget
dimensions.description: Building a quantitative model of where cycles are spent and what the theoretical floor is (given slot limits, SIMD width, dependency chains), and using it to target the <1250 budget.
dimensions.why_it_matters: This is an aggressive numeric target, not a vague 'faster'. Reaching <1250 from 147,734 requires reasoning about the achievable lower bound — how many bundles the computation must take given parallelism and slot constraints — to know which optimizations can possibly close the gap and when the agent is near the floor. This quantitative bottleneck analysis is distinct from generic progress tracking or correctness checking.

anchors.0: Optimizes blindly with no notion of where cycles go or what's achievable.
anchors.3: Hand-wavy sense that 'vectorizing helps' without quantifying the dominant cost or any floor.
anchors.5: Identifies the dominant cycle consumers (e.g. per-round hash-stage work × batch) and reasons roughly about how much a transform can save.
anchors.8: Constructs an explicit cost model tying instruction counts and slot occupancy to cycles, estimates a theoretical lower bound, and uses the gap between measured and floor to prioritize the next optimization.
anchors.10: Derives a tight lower-bound cycle model from slot limits, SIMD width, and critical-path dependencies, uses it to decide which transforms are worth attempting and to recognize when the kernel is near-optimal — turning a blind search into a directed descent toward the budget.
